title: CIPHER: Contextual Instruction Precedence and Hierarchy Evaluation for Repositories

authors.name: Awaiz Ahmed

abstract: Repository instruction files such as AGENTS.md guide AI coding agents, and a nested file may legitimately refine or replace guidance from its ancestors, so an apparent disagreement is not necessarily a defect. CIPHER defines a task-conditioned classification of instruction pairs under a declared directory-precedence profile into five labels: unresolved conflict, valid override, disjoint applicability, compatible, and insufficient evidence. From a public configuration dataset we built a traceable pilot set of 27 real instruction pairs from eight repositories at pinned commits, each with a context-changing variant and an order control, and a blinded annotation protocol. Human reference labels have not yet been collected, so this short paper reports a preliminary analysis, frozen by hash before predictions were opened, that needs none: accuracy on the 21 originals and variants whose label the profile fixes from file paths, and label-free measures elsewhere. With one local open-weight model, a direct prompt given the full evidence and a structured pipeline that computes applicability and precedence explicitly were both correct on all 21 profile-determined cases, whereas a keyword heuristic flagged 2 of 26 such cases as conflicts. No model judged any original or variant to be an unresolved conflict; the methods disagreed mainly on condition-based applicability, and swapping only the order of the two instructions changed 4 of 27 predictions for each model arm. The structured pipeline used more output tokens than the direct prompt (3589 versus 2177 per case) without a measurable gain. Human labels for the semantic cases are the next step.
status: Preliminary results without human labels (profile-determined subset and label-free measures)
